items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The write_to_file diff is empty in the trajectory, so the code itself can't be checked. The final message describes a queue and worker pool with reasonable structure, but naming and comments can't be verified as better than average.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: It hand-rolls an asyncio.Queue worker pool, sized min(max_concurrent, len(tasks)), plus manual cancel and gather instead of a Semaphore with a TaskGroup. That is more custom lifecycle code than needed, though it is reportedly compact.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: It cancels workers on interrupt and awaits them with gather(*workers, return_exceptions=True), then re-raises the original error. Exceptions raised during that cleanup are collected and dropped silently. It uses a broad catch-all for any exception. It does validate max_concurrent < 1.

items.name: Failures and degenerate arguments
items.evidence: Pre-write tests show `if not tasks: return` and `if max_concurrent < 1: raise ValueError`. In the failure test, 'Task 2 cleanup done' runs and then 'Caught exception: Task failed' surfaces. The queue-drain test passed and workers are awaited, so no tasks leak.

items.name: Required signature and import behaviour
items.name_zh: 签名与导入行为符合要求
items.evidence: `from run import run_tasks` imports with no side effects and uses only the stdlib. Workers call each zero-argument callable only when they pull it off the queue, so a task starts only when a slot is free. The concurrency-limit test and all 6 hidden tests pass.
